Lesion study · switch-level model

What breaks when one transistor fails

Each of the 4004's 2,242 transistors was forced permanently off (stuck open) and, separately, permanently on (stuck closed) in a transistor-level simulation of the chip, and the damaged chip was put through 2,046 single-instruction tests and 3 reset tests. Hover or tap a transistor to see what its loss breaks.

Transistor

Hover over the die (or tap) to inspect a transistor. Click to keep it selected.

How to read it

Severity. Global: the instructions used to set up and read back the chip fail, or 240+ of the 256 opcodes fail on some test. Broad: 12+ of 19 instruction groups fail (usually a data or address bit). Partial: fewer groups (instruction-specific). Reset-only: only the reset tests differ.

Instructions list the share of that instruction's tests that fail. Kinds say what went wrong: ACC/CY/REG (data), PC/STACK, CMRAM/CM (command lines), ADDR/MBUS/X1/XDOC/DRV (bus), XUND (undocumented X2/X3 bus contents only), SYNC, UNST (simulator did not settle).

Clusters group transistors whose lesions break the same set of instructions in the same ways. Blocks are named from the intact chip's behaviour (a node that always equals register R5 bit 2 belongs to the index registers), not from a drawing.

What "no effect" means here

The simulator treats transistors as ideal switches: no voltages, no leakage, no delays, and a path to ground always beats a path to the supply. So no effect means no difference on the pins in these tests, in this model. It does not mean the transistor is unnecessary.

  • A load stuck on, or a protection device stuck off, changes nothing by construction.
  • A stuck-on device fighting another is resolved as a clean 0 (flag contention); silicon would give a bad level.
  • A node left without a driver keeps its charge forever (flag floats); silicon would leak it away within milliseconds.
  • The test rig drives TEST, RESET and the clocks as ideal sources.
